title: Attention, Please! Revisiting Attentive Probing Through the Lens of Efficiency
claim: Standard attentive probing needs separate query, key and value projections; ours drops the redundant ones and uses learned queries directly.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right data flow, shared tensor-block notation
description: Two gray panels sit side by side. Each shows a cross-attention block built from 3D stacked tensor blocks. Patch tokens X (N×D_i, light blue stack) sit at the lower left. A query u (pink) is at the top. Colored stacks stand for keys K and values V (blue), the attention map a (orange columns), and the output y, the global representation (green). In the left panel, weight matrices W_Q, W_K and W_V project u and X into q, K and V. The arrows then go through a ⊗ and softmax to a, and a second ⊗ gives y. In the right panel the query projection and key projection are removed. Learned multi-query vectors u (M rows) are used directly, and X serves as the keys. Only W_V stays. The eye goes first to the colorful tensors and the simplified arrows on the right. The bottom of the V stacks looks slightly clipped, and the panel labels are missing. The caption describes a training-curve plot, not this diagram.
caption: Validation top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K over training epochs for EP, with and without the auxiliary attention-similarity loss. The additional loss slightly accelerates early training but both variants converge to identical final performance.
abstract: As fine-tuning becomes impractical at scale, probing is emerging as the preferred evaluation protocol. However, standard linear probing can understate the capability of models whose pre-training optimizes local representations rather than an explicit global representation. This motivates attentive probing, an alternative that uses attention to selectively aggregate patch-level features. Despite growing adoption, attentive probing is still underexplored: existing approaches are often over-parameterized and computationally inefficient. In this work, we revisit attentive probing through the lens of the accuracy vs. parameter-efficiency trade-off. We present the first comprehensive study of existing methods, analyzing their design choices and benchmarking their performance. Building on these insights, we propose efficient probing (EP), a lightweight yet effective multi-query cross-attention mechanism that eliminates redundant projections and reduces the number of trainable parameters. Across multiple benchmarks and pre-training paradigms, EP consistently outperforms linear probing and previous attentive probing methods, and remains effective when combined with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Beyond evaluation, our analysis uncovers emerging properties of EP, including complementary attention maps, which open new directions for leveraging probing beyond protocol design.
